extracted.intended_audience: readers and practitioners of art and aesthetics (artists, critics, students of literature and music)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical principles for judging or producing genuine art across media (literature, music, painting, drama), emphasizing transmission of feeling, artistic integrity, and signs of counterfeit art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as transmission of feeling (infection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist, if a real artist, has by his work transmitted to others the feeling he experienced. If a work be good as art, then the feeling expressed by the artist—be it moral or immoral—transmits itself to other people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If transmitted to others, then they feel it, and all interpretations are superfluous. If the work does not infect people, no explanation can make it contagious. The interpretation of works of art by words only indicates that the interpreter is himself incapable of feeling the infection of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics' incapacity and the perversion of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic criticism is often the valuation of art by erudite individuals who, being less susceptible than others to the contagion of art, interpret rather than feel works of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics' writings contribute to perverting public taste because they eulogise 'brain-spun, invented works' and set up authorities and traditions which later artists copy; criticism thus promotes counterfeits by praising works the critics cannot themselves be infected by.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism fosters counterfeit art
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionalism is the first condition of the diffusion of false, counterfeit art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When artists live by the trade—receiving remuneration through editors, publishers, impresarios and intermediaries—art becomes a profession and methods for producing imitation and marketable works proliferate, encouraging counterfeits rather than genuine artistic transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art schools teach imitation, not the creation of art
rubrics_metrics.description: No school can evoke feeling in a man; the one thing these schools can teach is how to transmit feelings experienced by other artists in the way those other artists transmitted them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools teach drawing from copies and models, composition by giving themes treated by former masters, recitation as earlier tragedians declaimed, and music theory as repetition of past methods. 'The teaching of the schools stops there where the _wee bit_ begins—consequently where art begins.' Thus schools produce counterfeits and disaccustom people from understanding real art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art consists of infinitely minute degrees (precision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic perfection depends on infinitesimally small adjustments—'a wee bit'—in execution which cannot be taught by external means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In music the three chief conditions for artistic execution are pitch, time, and strength: the exact centre of the required note, exact duration, and exact strength. The slightest deviation in pitch, timing, or strength destroys perfection and the 'infectiousness' of the work. Analogues exist in painting (tone, position), drama (timing, emphasis), and poetry (word arrangement). These minute degrees are found only by feeling, not by instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and indivisibility of a true work of art
rubrics_metrics.description: A true work of art has such entirety and completeness that the smallest alteration in its form would disturb the meaning of the whole work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In genuine art it is impossible to extract one line, scene, figure, or bar and relocate it without infringing the significance of the whole—just as one cannot transplant an organ without damaging an organism. If parts can be transposed without altering sense, this indicates a counterfeit (as argued about Wagner's later music where transpositions do not alter musical sense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from preconceived demand (no forced adjustment)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the chief conditions of artistic creation is the complete freedom of the artist from every kind of preconceived demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The necessity of adjusting a work to the demands of another art or to external preconceptions destroys creative power; works made to fit such constraints tend to be imitations or counterfeits rather than true art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods and signs of counterfeit art: borrowings, imitation, effects, interestingness
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfeit art is produced by methods such as borrowings, imitation, theatrical or sensational effects, and an emphasis on 'interestingness' rather than genuine feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods—exemplified in the essay's critique of Wagner—combine subject borrowings, imitative decoration, striking effects (monsters, magic fires, spectacle), and contrived 'interest' to manufacture apparent artistic value rather than transmit feeling. Recognition of these methods helps distinguish counterfeit from true art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility (generally) of fully uniting distinct arts (e.g., music and drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each art has its own definite realm; if two arts (dramatic and musical) are united in one production, the demands of one will make it impossible to fulfil the demands of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lyric poetry and music may coincide because both aim to produce a mental condition, but epic or dramatic poetry cannot be fully reconciled with music. Attempts to make both 'appear in full strength' (as Wagner proposed) are argued to produce counterfeits, unless the result degenerates into imitation or illustration rather than true art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial predetermination and prescribed emotion undermine art
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author prescribes the audience's emotion in advance ('Prepare to cry or to laugh'), the audience is prevented from genuinely experiencing the feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author's evident predetermination or insistence that the audience be moved breeds distrust and resistance; emotional manipulation and obvious contrivance (e.g., forced poetic moments or stage effects) impede the natural infection that constitutes real artistic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical indicators of unintelligibility or counterfeit composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain musical traits—absence of melody, continual commencements that are not continued, over-complication of harmony and orchestration, and music serving only to illustrate words—indicate a work's failure to infect and thus its counterfeit nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the text include Wagner's use of repeated leit-motifs tied strictly to words and things, long chant-like declamation instead of melody, and music that seems to begin musical thoughts only to break them off; such characteristics make the music obscure, unintelligible, and insufficient to produce genuine artistic infection.
